I searched the ChargeOps technical knowledge base for guidance on “OCPP charger repeatedly loses connectivity” but did not retrieve any sufficiently relevant KB articles. The list below is therefore general best-practice troubleshooting (inference), not direct KB citations.

Recommended checklist — what to check when an OCPP charger repeatedly loses connectivity

1. Verify basic network reachability
- From the charger (or its gateway) run ping/traceroute to the CSMS hostname/IP to confirm intermittent packet loss or routing problems.  
- Confirm DNS resolution of the CSMS hostname (nslookup/dig).

2. Inspect OCPP / connectivity logs
- Check the charger’s OCPP logs for repeated errors: heartbeat/connection lost, TLS handshake failures, authentication errors (401/403), WebSocket close codes.  
- Record timestamps of disconnects to correlate with network events or server logs.

3. Heartbeat / keepalive / timeout settings
- Verify the configured OCPP heartbeat/keepalive interval and server-side timeouts. A mismatched/too-short timeout can cause perceived disconnects.  
- Check whether TCP keepalive (or WebSocket pings) are enabled and appropriate for NAT timeouts on the path.

4. TLS / certificate issues
- Check certificate validity/expiry and full chain on the charger and CSMS.  
- Use openssl s_client (or device TLS logs) to inspect handshake and cipher negotiation issues that could cause disconnects.

5. NAT, firewall, and port connectivity
- Ensure required ports (typically 443 for WSS/TLS or configured port) are allowed and persistent NAT mappings are maintained.  
- Check firewall logs for dropped connections or throttling and confirm no deep-packet-inspection is terminating long-lived connections.

6. Cellular / SIM / radio issues (if cellular)
- Check SIM status, APN configuration, data plan validity, and operator reliability.  
- Inspect signal strength (RSSI/RSRP/RSRQ) and any modem logs for registration or handover problems.  
- Check for roaming or operator-imposed session timeouts and consider using a static APN settings or keepalive strategy.

7. Router / upstream equipment
- Check for router or NAT session timeouts that close idle TCP connections; lengthen timeouts or use keepalives.  
- Verify MTU settings — fragmentation problems can break TLS/WebSocket sessions (test with ping -M do).

8. Server/CSMS side: capacity and session handling
- Review CSMS logs for connection limits, throttling, or crashes at the times of disconnection.  
- Verify that the server accepts long-lived WebSocket/TCP sessions and is not periodically restarting or rebalancing connections.

9. Firmware / software bugs
- Confirm charger firmware, modem firmware, and TLS library versions. Check vendor release notes for known connectivity bugs and apply recommended updates or hotfixes.

10. Time synchronization
- Ensure the charger’s clock is accurate (NTP). Large clock skew can cause TLS certificate validation failures.

11. Network quality / congestion
- Check for high latency, packet loss, jitter on the access link. Use continuous ping or iperf where possible to detect patterns (time-of-day congestion).

12. Diagnostics and captures
- Enable verbose/debug logging on the charger and CSMS.  
- Capture packet traces (tcpdump) during an event to see TLS handshake failures, TCP resets, or WebSocket close frames.  
- Collect modem logs (AT logs), system logs, and exact timestamps for escalation.

13. Environmental and power checks
- Verify stable power supply and temperature — some devices restart or have flaky radios when overheating or undervoltage occurs.

14. Operational mitigations
- If intermittent cellular coverage is suspected, consider alternative connectivity (ethernet/fixed wireless) or a redundant SIM.  
- Adjust heartbeat intervals or implement reconnect backoff to avoid connection storming.

Suggested next actions
- Collect a short timeline of disconnects (timestamps) and pull charger OCPP/TLS logs and a network packet capture for at least one failure.  
- If you want, I can: (a) run a focused KB search again with a different query; or (b) guide you through specific commands/log locations to collect the diagnostic data; or (c) if this is for station KL-205, fetch station details and recent incidents to do a station-specific diagnosis.

Knowledge sources
- No relevant ChargeOps KB articles were retrieved for this query. The checklist above is derived from general OCPP/network troubleshooting best practices (not KB citations).

Summary
- Station: KL-205 (ChargeOps Central), charger: ABB Terra 54 — diagnosis run for: "connector becomes unusually hot during charging."
- Severity: High. Confidence: ~82%.
- An incident was created and recorded: incident_id 15 (status: open).

Likely root causes (supported by knowledge base)
- Poor electrical contact / high contact resistance at plug/socket (worn/pitted contacts, loose mating) [KB1][KB3].  
- Contamination on contacts (dirt, corrosion, debris) increasing resistance [KB1].  
- Damage to cable or internal conductor (melting, broken strands) or damaged connector housing [KB1].  
- Impaired cooling / reduced thermal margin (blocked vents, failed fans, high ambient temperature) contributing to overheating [KB2][KB3][KB5].  
- Faulty or mis-reporting temperature sensor (less likely but possible) [KB2].

Immediate safety actions (do these first)
1. Stop charging and isolate the outlet immediately. Prevent further use of the affected connector until inspected. This reduces risk of fire or equipment damage.  
2. Cordon off the area and warn users; place out-of-service signage.  
3. Record the event time, vehicle ID (if available), displayed fault codes, and connector temperature if a reading is available.

Short diagnostic checklist for a field technician (in order)
1. Visual inspection: look for discoloration, burns, melting, pitting, or foreign material on plug and socket. If you see arcing, burning, or severe damage, remove from service and escalate. (KB1)  
2. Verify mechanical fit: ensure the plug fully seats and the latch/lock functions correctly; a partially engaged plug raises contact resistance (KB1).  
3. Inspect cable and strain relief for cuts, crushed areas, or heat damage; examine conductor insulation if visible (KB1).  
4. Check cooling/ventilation: confirm vents are clear, fans are spinning, and filters are not clogged (KB2, KB3).  
5. Review charger logs/alarms: capture thermal fault codes and timestamps; do not repeatedly reset thermal faults (KB2).  
6. If qualified and safe to do so: measure contact resistance and continuity with appropriate instruments and PPE. Compare to known-good baseline/spec. Elevated contact resistance confirms poor contact or conductor damage.  
7. If contamination is present and manufacturer-approved cleaning procedures exist, clean contacts per ABB guidance and retest (KB3).  
8. After any repair/cleaning: run a short, monitored charging session while observing connector temperature and logs. If temperatures remain high or faults recur, remove from service.

When to take the outlet/charger out of service
- Evidence of electrical arcing, melted material, heavy pitting, or cable/conductor damage.  
- Recurrent over-temperature events after cleaning/inspection or failed cooling components.  
- Inability to verify safe contact resistance or replace/repair degraded components on-site.  
(If removed from service, escalate for parts replacement or factory-level service per ABB Terra procedures.) [KB1][KB2][KB3]

Documentation and escalation
- Log all findings, measured temperatures, test readings, photos of damage, and actions taken. The incident (ID 15) is open and should be updated with field notes.  
- Escalate immediately if you find evidence of arcing, severe damage, or if a safe repair cannot be completed on-site.

Evidence vs. inference
- The specific causes and cooling-related checks are supported by knowledge-base documents [KB1], [KB2], [KB3], [KB5].  
- The ordered immediate actions, measurement steps, and escalation thresholds are a structured synthesis of that guidance plus standard electrical safety and field-practice inference.

- KB2: Charger Over-Temperature Troubleshooting — ChargeOps Demo Knowledge Base.  
- KB3: ABB Terra Test Manual — test-ev-manual.txt.  
- KB5: Environmental Effects on EV Chargers — ChargeOps Demo Knowledge Base.

These incidents repeatedly point at thermal-management problems (cooling, connector/contact heating) often correlated with network disconnects.

Summary assessment (evidence vs inference)
- Evidence from the incident history: repeated over-temperature shutdowns and OCPP session drops at KL-101 across several recent incidents (high severity, open). This is direct operational evidence from the station record.
- Technical guidance from the ChargeOps knowledge base (supporting recommendations below): thermal faults commonly come from blocked airflow, failed fans, dirty filters, degraded temperature sensors, high contact resistance at connectors or cable damage; OCPP drops are commonly network-layer issues but can also be caused by thermal-induced component throttling or shutdowns [KB1, KB2, KB3, KB5]. High ambient temperature can reduce cooling margin and contribute [KB4].
- Inference / remaining uncertainty: The most likely causes are impaired cooling or connector/contact heating, possibly combined with network instability. Root cause cannot be confirmed without onsite measurements and log correlation.

Recommended immediate actions (priority order)
1. Keep the station in maintenance (it already is). Do not return to service until inspections and measurements are completed. (Safety-first.)
2. Onsite inspection checklist (high priority)
   - Inspect and clear ventilation paths and intake/exhaust vents; clean/replace filters.
   - Verify cooling fans are running and at spec (visual, audible, tachometer if available).
   - Inspect connector and cable: check for contamination, visible damage, wear, and loose connections.
   - Measure connector contact temperature during a controlled charge attempt (if safe to do so).
   - Inspect internal temperature sensors for error codes or abnormal readings.
   - Check enclosure sealing for ingress/humidity if applicable.
   (KB2, KB3)
3. Measurements and logs to collect
   - Charger internal ambient temperatures and sensor logs around the time of faults.
   - Connector/contact temperatures (IR thermography recommended).
   - Fan rpm and airflow measurements if possible.
   - DC/AC connection contact resistance and cable insulation condition.
   - Charger event logs and timestamps for over-temp and session drops.
   - Network logs: modem signal strength, WAN interface stats, ping/traceroute to backend, TLS/session errors.
   (KB1, KB5)
4. Temporary mitigations (while diagnosing)
   - Keep station out of service (maintenance) and tag it so customers can’t start sessions.
   - If onsite testing is required, perform controlled tests with supervision and logging rather than returning to normal use.
   - If connector heating is localized to a single cable, remove/replace that cable before returning to service.
   (KB2, KB3)
5. Escalation criteria
   - If over-temperature persists after cleaning vents/filters and confirming fans/sensors are functional → escalate to Siemens support / qualified field technician for component replacement.
   - If OCPP/backend connectivity problems remain after verifying modem/signal/DNS/TLS and replacing suspect hardware → escalate to network/backend team and vendor.
   (KB1, KB5)
